blocks.x: What is happening

A planned headquarters move has put Winnipeg office vacancy in the news. [Wealth Professional](https://www.wealthprofessional.ca/investments/alternative-investments/ig-wealth-future-exit-could-drive-winnipeg-office-vacancy-past-19/393742), citing Colliers' Q3 2026 research, reported that IG Wealth Management plans to move from its 280,904-square-foot headquarters at 447 Portage Avenue to 360 Main Street. [IG expects its move to run to mid-2028](https://www.ig.ca/en/media-room/media-releases/ig-wealth-management-strengthens-commitment-to-winnipeg-with-new-downtown-headquarters) and plans to sell the building.

Wealth Professional's report of Colliers' Q3 2026 snapshot has Class B vacancy across Winnipeg rising from 13.8% to 19.1%. The report ties this to IG Wealth's planned exit from 447 Portage and says Colliers notes the adjustment correlates with a reorganization of its database.

[CBRE](https://mktgdocs.cbre.com/2299/635166d3-3766-4bba-836b-1640e9e191dc-610961676/Winnipeg_Office_Figures_Q3_202.pdf), using its own data, has downtown Class B at 19.5%, down 10 basis points in the quarter.

The broader market is mixed. Wealth Professional's report has Colliers' overall office vacancy at 14.1% in Q3, with negative absorption of 119,527 square feet. [CBRE's Q3 2026 figures](https://www.cbre.com/insights/figures/winnipeg-office-figures-q3-2026) put overall vacancy higher, at 15.1%, but falling, with 107,000 square feet of positive net absorption, the strongest since Q1 2024.
So the two firms disagree on how the quarter went, and Colliers' Class B figure carries that database note.
Why Winnipeg's Class B office buildings are under pressure
Class B buildings are typically older, with fewer amenities and less modern systems than Class A. In a market where tenants can upgrade, those buildings face competition from both directions:
**Class A buildings** with space still to fill.
**New or renovated suburban buildings** with parking and convenient access.
When a large tenant moves out of Class B, the space can be hard to re-lease in its existing condition. A floor built around one company's older layout may not match what today's tenants want.
Our view: Class B owners need a renovation strategy, not just a leasing strategy

Lower rents alone may not win tenants in a market with choices. Tenants compare the experience of the space: the lobby, the washrooms, the light, the layout. [Office renovations](/services/office-renovations) that close the gap with Class A can make a Class B building competitive at a lower price point, which is what many cost-conscious tenants want.
Priorities for Class B owners:
**Common areas first.** Lobbies, elevator areas, corridors and washrooms shape every visitor's impression.
**Spec suites.** Pre-built, move-in-ready suites are easier to show than raw space, and many small and mid-size tenants do not want to manage a fit-out.

**Demising large floors.** Large single-tenant floors often need to be divided into smaller suites. Check what that means for [permits and occupancy](/blog/occupancy-permit-change-of-use-winnipeg) first.
**Envelope and windows.** Drafty windows and dated façades undermine everything inside.
**Flexible finishes.** Durable flooring, neutral paint and adaptable layouts can reduce future tenant improvement costs.
The demolition question

A vacant Class B floor can need significant [interior demolition](/services/demolition) before it can be re-leased: removing old offices, ceilings and finishes to create open, flexible space. That work is often the first step in a re-positioning program, and doing it ahead of leasing lets landlords show tenants the potential of the space.
In older buildings, have suspect materials tested before anything comes down. Our guide covers [asbestos testing before renovating](/blog/asbestos-testing-before-renovating-manitoba).
Conversion as an option

Some older office buildings are better suited to other uses. In 2022 a city councillor [proposed making it easier](https://www.ctvnews.ca/winnipeg/article/turning-an-office-into-a-home-the-citys-new-idea-to-get-people-living-downtown/) to turn vacant downtown offices into homes. A later [Vacant Building Grant](https://www.winnipeg.ca/building-development/housing/housing-accelerator-fund/vacant-building-grant), part of the City's Housing Accelerator Fund work, accepted conversions from office use until intake closed on August 17, 2026.

In January 2026, [CBRE noted one building slated to become a hotel on Broadway](https://www.cbre.com/insights/articles/whats-ahead-for-winnipeg-commercial-real-estate-in-2026), and said that was the extent of it. Not every building can be converted, and a change of use brings its own permit steps, but owners should evaluate the option alongside renovation.
What tenants are likely to ask

Expect tenants touring Class B space to ask practical questions: Can we move in quickly? Are the washrooms updated? Is there natural light? Can the layout be changed without major cost? Owners who can answer yes, with photos of finished suites and renovated common areas, will be better placed on those tours.

The IG move is still ahead, which gives Class B owners time to prepare. [IG says](https://www.ig.ca/en/media-room/media-releases/ig-wealth-management-strengthens-commitment-to-winnipeg-with-new-downtown-headquarters) it wants a new owner to redefine the building's purpose, so not all of that space may return as offices.
Space that is renovated before a large block comes back on the market should be better positioned than space renovated in response to it.
A sample re-positioning sequence

For a typical vacant Class B floor, a sensible sequence might look like this. First, once any suspect materials have been tested and dealt with, strip out the previous tenant's offices and ceilings so the floor shows its windows and volume. Next, renovate the elevator lobby and washrooms on that floor.

Then build one or two spec suites to demonstrate the finished product, leaving the rest of the floor flexible for larger tenants. Marketing can start as soon as the strip-out is done. This staged approach can spread cost and get space in front of tenants sooner.
The bottom line

Class B office in Winnipeg is not obsolete, but it is under pressure. Owners who invest in targeted office renovations, starting with common areas and move-in-ready suites, can compete for cost-conscious tenants even with vacancy at these levels.
